title: Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
authors: NED AUGENBLICK; EBEN LAZARUS
abstract: ABSTRACT We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral ) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

title: Pay‐for‐prominence: The (un)intended consequences of monetary incentives on employees' networks and attrition
authors: Alessandro Iorio; Giuseppe Soda; Brandy Aven
affiliations: Department of Management and Technology Bocconi University Milan Italy; ICRIOS Bocconi University Milan Italy; Tepper School of Business Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We introduce the concept of pay‐for‐prominence , a system where employees are monetarily incentivized to become knowledge hubs in the intrafirm network and examine its effects on employees' networks and attrition. Integrating social network theory with relational incentives theory, we argue that pay‐for‐prominence motivates strategic networking behaviors that lead to the emergence of prominent connectors. However, these changes are associated with higher attrition as employees are preoccupied with networking, thus suggesting a trade‐off between enhanced connectivity in the short term and the risk of network fragmentation in the long term. Using a field quasi‐experiment in a multinational firm, we show that organizations can successfully incentivize employees' network prominence, but doing so may produce unintended consequences. Managerial Summary We examine the impact of using monetary incentives to encourage employees to become knowledge hubs in the workplace informal network—a term we label pay‐for‐prominence. We find that offering monetary rewards based on network metrics encourages employees to broaden their connections, enhancing knowledge flows within the firm. However, employees who become more socially prominent experience higher attrition than those who do not, as they become preoccupied with networking. Therefore, while incentivizing networking can improve knowledge sharing, it also requires careful management to avoid unintended consequences, such as the exit of key players that could cause fragmentation of the social network. Managers should weigh the benefits of increased connectivity against the risks of fragmentation when designing incentive programs aimed at fostering informal networks.

title: Public Administration and the Crisis of American Democracy
authors: Donald F. Kettl
affiliations: University of Maryland School of Public Policy College Park Maryland USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The field of public administration stands amid genuine crisis. Americans don't trust government or its administrators. Elected officials have attacked the career service as agents of the “deep state” and, though it might be hard to admit, many of public administration's critics have a point. Government's performance too often falls short of what people expect, practitioners too often seem too unresponsive to elected officials, and researchers too often seem to have only fuzzy guidance for practitioners. However, public administration undoubtedly is more important now than ever in translating public goals into effective action, and in bringing to life the democratic aspirations Madison and his colleagues wished for the country at its founding. The field urgently needs new strategies and tactics for solving the new generation of puzzles the country faces. In coming together, practitioners and researchers build on these puzzles to chart an exciting road forward.

title:
Everything everywhere all‐at‐once?
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    , expertise–output decoupling, and new entrepreneurial strategy trade‐offs in the age of abundance
authors: Jen Gennai; Riitta Katila; Minu Kumar; Ian Sinapuelas
affiliations: T3 Consultants New York New York USA; Microsoft Redmond Washington USA; Google Mountain View California USA; Stanford University Stanford California USA; San Francisco State University San Francisco California USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.

title: Inventory adjustment under global supply chain pressure: the moderating role of working capital structure
authors: Rahul Pandey; Farooq Durrani
affiliations: The University of Memphis Department of Supply Chain Management, , , ,; University of Louisville Department of Finance, , , ,
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate how global supply chain pressure affects firms' inventory adjustment and how this relationship depends on their working capital structure, specifically supplier trade credit, customer credit exposure, and liquidity. Design/methodology/approach We draw on organizational information processing theory and real options theory to develop hypotheses about how global supply chain pressure and working capital structure shape firm inventory adjustment. The hypotheses are tested using a panel of 214,674 firm-quarter observations from 6,499 publicly listed US manufacturing firms over 1998–2025. We employ a shift–share panel design with firm and quarter fixed effects for the empirical analysis. Findings The results reveal that firms increase inventory as global supply chain pressure rises, but the average buffering response masks substantial heterogeneity in how firms manage supply uncertainty. Firms with higher supplier trade credit and customer credit exposure respond more strongly by increasing inventory. Liquidity has the opposite effect. It weakens the inventory response and, at high levels, reverses it, indicating a shift toward flexibility preservation. Liquidity further conditions the role of supplier trade credit and customer credit exposure, such that supplier financing matters most when liquidity is scarce, whereas customer credit exposure becomes more consequential when liquidity is abundant. Originality/value This study contributes to inventory management research by integrating the buffering and flexibility preservation perspectives on inventory under uncertain supply chain conditions. It shows that rising global supply chain pressure does not uniformly lead firms to build inventory buffers. Instead, the balance between buffering and flexibility preservation depends on the working capital structure that supports or constrains inventory commitment. The study also advances a liquidity-centered account of inventory adjustment by showing that liquidity changes both the inventory response to global supply chain pressure and the roles of supplier financing and customer credit exposure in supporting inventory buffers under strained supply conditions.

title: Reshaping Work: Job Reallocation and Job Attributes During the Great Resignation in Italy
authors: Francesco Suppressa; Chiara Franco; Tiziano Razzolini
affiliations: University of Pisa Pisa Italy; University of Siena, GLO, IZA, LABOR, and ASESD Siena Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT The Covid‐19 pandemic reshaped labor markets worldwide, including the emergence of the “Great Resignation” (GR). This study examines whether Italy's GR reflects labor force exits or job switching and identifies and explores which job attributes are associated with these reallocation patterns. Using Italian Labor Force Survey data, we construct a job‐switching indicator that aligns with administrative resignation trends and enables the exploration of potential determinants through a task‐based approach. Results are consistent with the interpretation that Italy's Great Resignation mainly reflects job reallocation across occupations characterized by differences in flexibility, meaning, and working conditions.

title: The Symbolic Politics of Housing
authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN; CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF; JOSHUA L. KALLA
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley; University of California, Davis; Yale University
abstract: Voter opposition to development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize NIMBYism (opposition to housing nearby) and homeowners’ self-interest. However, homeownership often fails to predict housing policy views, while NIMBYism offers little insight into support for policies that do not concern specific proposed housing projects—the focus of much recent policymaking. Drawing on symbolic politics theory, we argue that voters’ affect toward groups that housing policies make salient powerfully shapes their judgments about housing policies. We present evidence supporting this theory. Experiments show that affect toward developers and investors who build housing, government actors who approve it, and residents who move into it explain anti-development preferences when policies make these groups salient. Providing further causal evidence, short-form videos that manipulate affect toward developers have meaningful downstream effects on support for new development and permitting reforms. Ironically, voter dislike of the very actors who could ameliorate the housing shortage further exacerbates it.

title: Share Issues vs. Share Repurchases
authors: Philip Bond; Yue Yuan; Hongda Zhong
affiliations: Foster School of Business, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; and Finance Theory Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Finance Theory Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; and School of Management and Department of Economics, University College London, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom; Finance Theory Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; and University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080; and The Centre for Economic Policy Research, London, EC1R 5HL, United Kingdom
abstract: Almost all firms repurchase shares through open-market repurchase programs. In contrast, issue methods are more diverse; at-the-market offerings, analogous to open-market repurchases, and seasoned equity offerings, analogous to rarely used tender-offer repurchases, are both used by significant fractions of firms. Furthermore, average seasoned equity offerings are larger than at-the-market offerings. We show that this asymmetry in the diversity of transaction methods in issuances and repurchases and the size-method relation in issuances are natural consequences of the single informational friction of a firm having superior information to investors. Moreover, although this friction always leads firms to issue inefficiently little, it leads firms to repurchase too little if they maximize long-term shareholder value but too much if the primary goal is to boost short-term share prices. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: Y. Zhong acknowledges support from the Economic and Social Research Council [New Investigator Grant ES/T003758/1]. title: Buffering institutional erosion: organizational ties and SME exports under populism
authors: Xiaolong Shui; Luyang Chen; Michael A. Witt
abstract: Abstract We argue that pre-existing organizational ties can partially buffer against the adverse effects of populist deinstitutionalization. In contrast with the chronic institutional weakness emphasized in prior literature, populist deinstitutionalization reflects a politically driven weakening of institutions that firms had previously relied on. This disrupts established routines and increases the transaction costs of cross-border exchange. For SMEs, which are highly dependent on external institutional support for internationalization, pre-existing ties to government actors, international suppliers, and foreign owners can provide partial buffering by replacing some of the coordination, information, and enforcement functions lost through institutional erosion. We test these arguments using data on 10,399 SMEs across 29 economies in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The results support our theoretical expectations: while populism is negatively associated with SME exporting, pre-existing organizational ties attenuate this adverse association, with foreign ownership providing the strongest buffering effect. Our findings extend institution-based research by identifying politically driven institutional erosion as a distinct challenge for international business and by showing that organizational ties can function as selective, imperfect buffers rather than substitutes for formal institutions.

Slavery and Northeastern Industrialization
authors: Sven Beckert; Mark Stelzner
affiliations: Department of History Harvard University Cambridge Massachusetts USA; Department of Economics Connecticut College New London Connecticut USA
abstract: Abstract From the 1820s through the 1850s, parts of New England began industrializing. Over the same period, slavery expanded in the southern states in terms of the number enslaved, the geography it encompassed, and the amount each enslaved worker produced. While many scholars have looked at the connections between northern industrialization and southern slavery, it is our aim in this paper to better identify the links between these two crucial developments in our nation's history by estimating the importance of the southern market for northern textiles – the key manufacturing industry during the early antebellum period. As we will see, the South was a crucial market for cotton textiles produced in America's first factories.

title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    and the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantages
authors: Haiyang Zhang; Robert Wuebker; Jay B. Barney
affiliations: Harvard Business School Boston Massachusetts USA; University of Utah Salt Lake City Utah USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantage. We argue that GenAI's impact is conditional on how those opportunities are formed. Discovery opportunities originate from exogenous industry shocks. However, widely available GenAI tools are likely to commoditize opportunity recognition in these settings and thus reduce advantages that might have been generated by exploiting these opportunities. Creation opportunities emerge endogenously, under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, through entrepreneurial action and interaction with the environment. However, GenAI cannot fully resolve the Knightian uncertainty inherent in creation settings, so sustained advantage here depends on whether resources and capabilities developed through creating an opportunity are inimitable. Unawareness opportunities rely on competitive neglect. GenAI may reduce the advantages of firms in these settings when it makes rents legible to potential competitors and when search is directed toward these invisible markets. Managerial Summary Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT and Claude help entrepreneurs spot opportunities, but every competitor can potentially access the same tools. Whether GenAI can create sustained competitive advantages, this paper argues, depends on how an opportunity is formed. When opportunities arise from entrepreneurs noticing an external market shift, GenAI levels the playing field by commoditizing recognition and pushes entrepreneurs to win through execution and hard‐to‐copy complements. When opportunities are created through actions and interactions of entrepreneurs with their environments, GenAI does not fully remove the uncertainty that makes these efforts entrepreneurial but can speed up experimentation. When opportunities emerge from entrepreneurs operating in markets neglected by competitors, GenAI may have a limited effect on advantage unless it makes invisible markets publicly known.

title: Offshore financial centres and banks’ funding responses to liquidity shocks
authors: Stefano Maiani; Barbara Casu; Angela Gallo; Alexandros Kontonikas
affiliations: Edinburgh Business School, Heriot-Watt University , Edinburgh, EH14 4AS,; Bayes Business School, City University of London , London, EC1Y 8TZ,; Essex Business School, University of Essex , Colchester, CO4 3SQ,
abstract: Abstract This article rethinks financial embeddedness by examining how transnational banks respond to funding pressures through the infrastructures of offshore financial centres (OFCs). Using hand-collected information, we construct a novel dataset of European banks across six Eurozone countries from 2009–15. We show that during the sovereign debt crisis, banks engaged in latent network activation, mobilizing offshore conduit arrangements to secure foreign currency funding as market conditions tightened, even when official liquidity support was available. We argue that embeddedness in global finance is dynamic and crisis-contingent, since relationships and organizational infrastructures that appear peripheral in stable periods can become decisive under stress. OFCs emerge not as passive enablers of regulatory arbitrage, but as active infrastructures used by global banks to access cross-border liquidity when conventional funding channels become impaired. This has important implications for the governance and oversight of cross-border liquidity flows and off-balance-sheet funding structures.

title: Seasonal Multivariate and Spatial Assessment of Heavy Metal Contamination and Associated Ecotoxicological and Human Health Risks in Urban Park Soils: A Case Study From Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
authors: Nguyen Xuan Tong; Le Thi Tuyen; Nguyen Kim Hoa; Luu Tang Phuc Khang
affiliations: Institute of Environmental Science, Engineering and Management Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh city Ho Chi Minh City Vietnam; Vo Van Kiet Highschool Ho Chi Minh City Vietnam; Ho Chi Minh University of Natural Resources and Environment Ho Chi Minh City Vietnam; Aquatic Biotechnology Laboratory, Department of Animal and Aquatic Sciences, Faculty of Agriculture Chiang Mai University Chiang Mai Thailand
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban parks in rapidly developing cities face increasing heavy metal contamination, yet seasonal dynamics remain poorly understood. This study evaluated seasonal variations in heavy metal contamination and associated human health risks in two major parks in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. We analyzed 48 surface soil samples (24 locations × 2 seasons) for eight metals using ICP‐OES. Pollution levels were evaluated using indices (EF, I geo , CF, PER, mHQ, TU, and TRI) and GIS‐geostatistics. Sources were apportioned via multivariate analysis and positive matrix factorization (PMF), and health risks to children and adults were simulated using Monte Carlo methods. Al (Go Vap 12,475 ppm; Gia Dinh 13,998 ppm) and Fe (Go Vap 12,324.1 ppm; Gia Dinh 7620.7 ppm) dominated soil composition. In Go Vap, there was an increase in Al, Mn enrichment and Pb spikes (EF = 91.69) in the dry season; Gia Dinh had Cr (EF = 4.43) enrichment in the dry season and higher Mn (EF = 4.19) in the rainy season. PMF identified four sources: traffic solid waste (31.4%), traffic emissions and construction dust (15.8%), natural weathering (20.1%), and redox processes (32.7%). Spatial analysis revealed dry‐season high‐risk hotspots expanding to 39.41% of Gia Dinh and 36.02% of Go Vap park areas. Cr posed the highest health risk (HQ = 0.53 for children, 0.057 for adults), primarily via ingestion. All risk indices intensified during the dry season ( p < 0.05). Dry seasons increase the risk of contamination in tropical urban parks, especially Cr. This study supports seasonal monitoring and enhanced protection for children in monsoon‐affected green spaces.

title: Modeling Exposure–Mortality Relationships for Indoor Heat
authors: Andrew Ibbetson; Charles Simpson; Giorgos Petrou; Eleni Oikonomou; Anna Mavrogianni; Rajat Gupta; Mike Davies; Ai Milojevic
affiliations: Institute for Environmental Design and Engineering, The Bartlett School of Environment, Energy and Resources University College London London UK; Low Carbon Building Research Group School of Architecture, Oxford Brookes University Oxford UK; Department of Public Health, Environments and Society, Faculty of Public Health and Policy London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine London UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Most individuals spend the majority of their time indoors. However, epidemiological evidence of the association between heat and mortality is dominated by studies using outdoor temperature as a proxy for personal exposure. To demonstrate how an exposure–response relationship between indoor heat and mortality may relate to that between outdoor heat and mortality, we develop a novel mathematical modeling approach. This approachuses the relationship between regional daily average indoor and outdoor temperature to map the exposure–response relationship for outdoor heat, estimated by epidemiological studies, to indoor heat. Due to the modifying effect of buildings on heat exposure, we show that a change in indoor temperature may be associated with a greater change in mortality than an equal change in outdoor temperature. This has implications for researchers seeking to assess the health impact of changes in indoor heat exposure. Furthermore, it provides a new theoretical framework for interpreting potential differences in the temperature‐mortality relationship of indoor and outdoor heat exposure in epidemiological studies.

title: Organization and the Signature of Power
authors: Mitchell Dean; Stefan Schwarzkopf
abstract: This paper introduces the ‘signature of power’ as a framework to enhance the understanding of politics in organizational studies. We argue for an understanding of contemporary forms of power as a signature that connects and divides two constellations: juridical-political sovereignty (supreme authority) on one side, and economic-managerial government (practical regulation) on the other. These poles have analogies in organizational theory dichotomies like formal versus informal, and institution versus network. The signature of power serves as a heuristic – a discovery mechanism – that enables scholars to navigate and integrate these opposing forces without reducing them to one dominant paradigm. The framework is articulated through four analytical strategies: analytics of government (local, immanent power practices), genealogy of order (historical foundations of governing orders), archaeology of glory (rituals and symbols of supreme authority), and analytics of authority (formal organizational hierarchies and operations). These strategies and their distinct relationships provide a more coherent analytical framework for a multi-paradigm approach to understanding power relations, resistance, and organizational forms. The paper tests this analytic framework through a study of the corporation as a ‘signature of power’ that bridges economic-managerial and juridical-political forms and is shaped by historical shifts and legal innovations. Addressing potential critiques, the paper emphasizes the framework’s adaptability to resistance and its applicability to diverse organizational contexts. This conceptualization encourages intellectual plurality, fostering historically and conceptually informed insight into politics as a set of power-related organizational and institutional practices.

title: Estimating Hysteresis Effects in Times of Crises
authors: VALERIE CERRA; MAI HAKAMADA; RUY LAMA; JUAN PABLO MEDINA
abstract: Abstract One of the most puzzling facts following the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) is that output in both advanced and emerging economies did not return to its pre‐crisis trend, contrary to the predictions of standard macroeconomic models. This paper analyzes the factors behind output hysteresis, with a special focus on the role played by financial crises. The paper shows that financial crises are associated with medium‐term output and total factor productivity (TFP) losses, suggesting that these crises lead to “scarring” effects on the supply side of the economy. The paper also examines how additional factors, such as persistently low investment rates, research and development (R&D), and the effects of currency and debt crises, contribute to these permanent losses. Our empirical findings are broadly consistent with models featuring endogenous productivity and capital‐embodied technological change, which suggest that a contraction in investment is a key factor that limits the adoption of new technologies, ultimately reducing medium‐term TFP and output.

title: It's in the Small Steps: Navigating Knotted Change‐Stability Tensions in Complex Collaborations
authors: Lea Stadtler; Luk N. Van Wassenhove
abstract: Abstract Addressing societal challenges requires collaborative arrangements that can adapt to changing environments while maintaining coherence. Existing research highlights collaborative responses to change, yet the processes through which such responses emerge remain poorly understood. Notably, collaborative change involves not only balancing change and stability but also navigating knotted collective‐individual tensions that arise in realigning interests, coordination structures, and operations. To advance understanding of these dynamics, we conduct an in‐depth longitudinal study of collaborative change in a cross‐sector disaster relief partnership. Across successive change stages, we identify stability drivers emerging from collective‐individual tensions that prompted the partners to adopt specific balancing practices. These practices enabled a change process that was incremental and fragile in progression, yet resilient in its cumulative pattern. We develop a process model that explains the dynamics of collaborative change and shows how balancing change and stability enables partners to progressively broaden and occasionally transcend collective‐individual alignment as trust and mutual understanding deepen. This study advances collaboration and paradox theory by exposing balancing practices tailored to collaborative settings that enable adaptation in dynamic environments and by proposing a gradual approach to navigating knotted paradoxes.

title: Building without income mixing: public housing quotas in France
authors: Guillaume Chapelle; Laurent Gobillon; Benjamin Vignolles
affiliations: CY Cergy Paris Université THEMA, , 33 Boulevard du Port , Cergy 95000,; Sciences Po LIEPP, , 27 rue Saint Guillaume , Paris, 75007,; Paris School of Economics CNRS, , 48 Boulevard Jourdan , Paris 75014,; Center for Economic and Policy Research , 187 Boulevard Saint Germain , Paris, 75007,; IZA Institute of Labor Economics , Schaumburg-Lippe-Straße 5-9 , Bonn, 53113,; Direction de la recherche, des études, de l'évaluation et des statistiques , 74-84 rue Olivier-de-Serres , Paris, 75015,
abstract: Abstract We study the effects of the SRU law introduced in France in December 2000 to support scattered development of public housing in cities and favor social mixity. This law imposes 20 per cent of public dwellings to all medium and large municipalities of large-enough cities, with fees for those not abiding by the law. Using exhaustive fiscal data, we evaluate the effects of the law over the 1996–2008 period using a difference-in-differences approach at the municipality and neighborhood levels. We find that the law stimulated public housing construction in treated municipalities, but only slightly increased the presence of low-income households. Indeed, new public dwellings enter categories to which medium-income are eligible and most additional occupants are not poor. Within municipalities, the policy decreased public housing segregation but it barely decreased low-income segregation. This comes from local authorities increasing over time the presence of public dwellings in neighborhoods away from existing public housing but in places concentrating low-income households.

title: Spanning boundaries to boost network engagement along implementation processes of digital technologies: evidence from a multiple case study in hospitals
authors: Vincent Peters; Bieke Henkens; Tom A. E. Aben; Melissa De Regge
affiliations: Tilburg University Department of Information Systems and Operations Management, , ,; Ghent University Department of Marketing, Innovation and Organization, , ,; Eindhoven University of Technology Department of Industrial Engineering and Innovation Sciences, , ,; Warwick Business School, University of Warwick , ,; University Hospital Ghent Strategic Policy Cell, , ,
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how boundary spanners realise network engagement during the implementation of digital technologies in healthcare operations, focusing on how actors connect diverse stakeholder groups across organisational, functional and professional boundaries. Design/methodology/approach A multiple case study was conducted in two hospitals implementing comparable digital technologies with contrasting outcomes. Data were collected through archival documents and two rounds of semi-structured interviews. By means of inductive analysis, we identified boundary-spanning roles and their contribution to network engagement across organisational, functional and professional boundaries. Findings The findings show that boundary-spanning roles operate not in isolation, but as a constellation that jointly activate, embed and legitimise across diverse groups of actors. Through this constellation, actors cross organisational, functional and professional boundaries, thereby supporting the implementation of digital technologies in healthcare operations. Originality/value This study contributes to healthcare operations literature by moving beyond single-organisation adoption models and introducing a network-based perspective on technology implementation. It advances boundary-spanning theory by conceptualising how boundary-spanning roles enable engagement across multi-actor networks, addressing a gap at the intersection of digital technology, healthcare operations and implementation. Practical principles are provided to guide managers in defining, supporting and leveraging boundary-spanning roles during technology implementation in healthcare operations.

title: Multi‐Agent Contracting With Network Externalities
authors: Yang Sun; Wei Zhao
affiliations: School of Economics Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu China; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper analyzes how the structure of externalities‐encompassing both pure spillovers and interactive components‐reshapes the classic trade‐off between incentives and risk in multi‐agent contracts. The interplay of network effects and moral hazard generates congestion effects among agents with a common neighbor, which we decompose into a sum of weighted Katz‐Bonacich centralities. This tractable characterization enables clear comparative statics on the externality structure. We further apply the framework to examine how organization structures shape firm boundaries, and the design of Pigovian taxes to generate social security.

title: Auditors' Response to Clients' Cyber Breaches: A Human‐Capital Perspective
authors: Bing Li; Yifu Li; Jeffrey Pittman; Wenfeng Wang
affiliations: Department of Accountancy City University of Hong Kong Kowloon Hong Kong; Department of Accounting Renmin University of China Beijing China; Faculty of Business Administration, Memorial University St. John's Newfoundland and Labrador Canada; Department of Accounting and Information Systems Virginia Tech Blacksburg Virginia USA; Department of Accounting Southern University of Science and Technology Shenzhen China
abstract: ABSTRACT Using online job postings data, we explore whether auditors adjust their human capital in response to clients' cyber breach incidents. We find that audit offices increase their demand for cybersecurity specialists after their clients' cyber breaches, implying that cyber breaches change not only client risk but also their auditor's production function. Consistent with expectations, we document that this impact is larger when breaches involve their own clients (rather than those of peer offices within the same audit firm) and when breaches directly involve financial information. Our evidence holds for both cyber‐focused and non‐cyber‐focused offices, highlighting the broad impact of cybersecurity risks on audit practices. Additionally, we find that audit offices with relatively high investment in cybersecurity human capital are better able to preserve their market share among clients in high‐cyber‐risk industries after a client's cyber breach.
